sentences.text: Last time, our count read the table with 4 tasks on 8 cores. Here's a worse case: the same 103 patients, written as one file.
Spark reads it with 1 task. One core works, and 7 sit idle.
Nothing is wrong with the data. It's how the rows are piled up.
Spark works pile by pile, and one file made one pile.
Welcome to Spark, Visually.
Today: piles of records.
Spark calls a pile of rows a partition. Each partition is worked on by one task, on one core, from start to finish.
Our 4 files make 4 piles. These two lines number each row's pile, and count them: 28, 25, 25 and 25.
Four piles: four cores work, and four sit idle.
Deal the rows into eight piles, and every core gets one. All eight work at once.
So why not 32 piles? The eight cores take the first eight. Whenever a core finishes, it takes the next pile.
Thirty-two piles run in four rounds.
This is a timeline: a lane for each core, and a bar for each task.
Every bar carries the same grey cap: the fixed cost of starting a task and wrapping it up.
Our piles hold about 3 patients each, so the cap is nearly the whole bar: more than 99 percent of each task is overhead.
For a simple count, a pile needs at least tens of thousands of rows before its real work matches that fixed cost.
So where do piles come from? When Spark reads files, it cuts big files into pieces, and packs small files together.
One big file of 61 megabytes, written in 8-megabyte row groups, became 8 piles, one for each core. And 32 small files became 8 piles too.
A piece is never bigger than 128 megabytes, and smaller when that gives every core a piece, but never under 4 megabytes.
Data you build in code starts as one pile per core.
And after a shuffle, a setting decides: 200 piles by default, unless Spark merges the small ones. That's episode 5.
To change the number of piles, there are two tools.
The first, coalesce, merges piles where they stand. Ours become two piles, of 53 and 50, and not one row is re-dealt.
The second, repartition, re-deals every row. All 103 go through a shuffle into eight new piles.
A shuffle has a real cost. We'll open one up in episode 5.
Piles don't have to be even. Write our cast as one big file and three small ones: piles of 70, 11, 11 and 11.
The big pile has over 6 times the rows. At scale, its core works on, while the others finish and wait.
A stage ends when its last task ends. One big pile holds up the whole job. Remember that. It comes back.
So how many piles? A few per core, each one big enough that its work dwarfs the fixed cost.
Too few, and cores sit idle. Too many tiny ones, and you pay for overhead. Uneven, and everyone waits for the biggest.
Let's gather it up.
A partition is a pile of rows, and one task works on one pile, on one core.
Files, code and shuffles decide the piles. Coalesce merges them, and repartition re-deals them.
One loose end: the coalesce and repartition lines returned instantly. Nothing ran until something asked for a result.
So when does Spark actually do the work? Next time: nothing happens until you ask.
This has been Spark, Visually. Thanks for watching the cluster with us.
